CWE-115.name: Misinterpretation of Input
CWE-115.question: Does this function misread an input in a way that changes a security decision, for example treating it as a different type, encoding, length or meaning than it has?

any: a value's type or format is guessed from an untrusted hint, such as a file extension, magic prefix or content-type header, and the guess drives a security check
a numeric or boolean value is parsed leniently (prefix parsing, truthy strings, partial matches) and the result grants or denies something
an encoded or escaped value is checked before decoding, so the checked form differs from the used form
input is parsed strictly against a defined format and rejected on any mismatch
the check is made on the same decoded, typed value that is later used
the interpretation has no security effect

distinguish_from.CWE-436: the misreading arises because a second component interprets the same data differently

CWE-435.name: Improper Interaction Between Multiple Correctly-Behaving Entities
CWE-435.question: Does this function combine its own logic with another component (parser, proxy, library, compiler, protocol peer) in a way where each could interpret the same data or behaviour differently?

any: the function parses, normalises or filters data that another component will parse again, such as HTTP messages, URLs, paths, filenames or file types
security decisions rely on assumptions about how a downstream server, client, library version or platform behaves
security-relevant code could be altered by compiler or runtime optimisation, such as clearing secrets or timing-safe comparisons
the function performs self-contained computation with no hand-off of parsed data or security assumption to another component
data is parsed once into a canonical form and only that form is passed on and checked

CWE-436.name: Interpretation Conflict
CWE-436.question: Does this function make a security decision about data or a request based on its own reading, when the component that later handles it may read it differently?

any: a filter, proxy, validator or scanner checks a raw value (URL, path, header, file extension, MIME type) and then passes the unmodified original on
the function's parser handles duplicates, encodings, case, separators or malformed parts differently from the downstream consumer
an access rule keyed on HTTP method, content type or extension assumes the backend treats them the same way
the value is canonicalised once and the same canonical value is both checked and forwarded
malformed or ambiguous input is rejected rather than interpreted
the function is the final consumer and makes no decision on another component's behalf

distinguish_from.CWE-444: the conflicting interpretation concerns HTTP message framing between an intermediary and a server
distinguish_from.CWE-650: access control assumes GET or other safe methods cannot change state
distinguish_from.CWE-115: the function itself misreads a single input with no second component involved

CWE-437.name: Incomplete Model of Endpoint Features
CWE-437.question: Does this intermediary or monitoring function make decisions based on an incomplete model of what an endpoint supports, so traffic using unmodelled features slips through or is mishandled?

any: a proxy, firewall, scanner or gateway inspects only some protocol features, encodings or commands and forwards anything else unchecked
a deny-list of methods, verbs, file types or message types is used where the endpoint accepts more variants than listed
state tracking for a protocol ignores endpoint features such as pipelining, compression, fragmentation or upgrades
the function forwards only an allow-list of features it fully understands and rejects the rest
the function is the endpoint itself, not an intermediary or monitor
unrecognised input is rejected rather than passed through

distinguish_from.CWE-444: the gap is specifically ambiguous HTTP message framing such as Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding

CWE-439.name: Behavioral Change in New Version or Environment
CWE-439.question: Does this function rely for safety on behaviour of a library, platform or peer that is undocumented, version-specific or known to have changed?

any: a security check depends on a particular default (encoding, sort order, TLS setting, parser leniency) that is not set explicitly
the code branches on a library, OS or protocol version string and assumes behaviour only for the versions it knows
a deprecated or removed API, flag or error code is relied on to enforce a restriction
security-relevant settings are configured explicitly rather than taken from defaults
unknown versions or unexpected behaviour lead to refusal rather than an assumption
the function's behaviour does not depend on another component's version or environment

distinguish_from.CWE-436: two components interpret the same data differently at the same time, without any version change

CWE-444.name: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')
CWE-444.question: Does this function parse or forward HTTP messages in a way that could frame the request or response boundary differently from the server or client on the other side?

any: a request carrying both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, or duplicate or conflicting Content-Length headers, is accepted and forwarded
header names or chunk sizes are parsed leniently (extra whitespace, odd casing, obsolete line folding, bare LF) instead of being rejected
a proxy or gateway forwards the raw header block or body while computing message length its own way
a reused backend connection is written to after a malformed or partially read message
ambiguous framing such as both length headers, duplicates or malformed chunk sizes is rejected with an error
the function relies on a mature HTTP library to parse and re-serialise the message rather than forwarding raw bytes
the function is not an HTTP intermediary or parser, only an application handler reading parsed fields

distinguish_from.CWE-436: the conflicting interpretation concerns something other than HTTP message framing
distinguish_from.CWE-437: the intermediary ignores endpoint features but message boundaries are not in question

CWE-650.name: Trusting HTTP Permission Methods on the Server Side
CWE-650.question: Does this function let a GET, HEAD or other supposedly safe HTTP request change state, while access controls or CSRF protection only cover methods such as POST?

any: a handler reachable by GET deletes, updates, creates or transfers data
authorisation or CSRF checks are applied only when the method is POST, PUT or DELETE, and the same action runs for other methods
a route accepts any method (or both GET and POST) for a state-changing action
state-changing actions are restricted to non-safe methods and protected by authorisation and CSRF checks
the GET handler only reads data that the caller is already authorised to see
the same access check runs regardless of HTTP method

CWE-1038.name: Insecure Automated Optimizations
CWE-1038.question: Does this function contain security-relevant code that a compiler, JIT or runtime optimiser could legally remove or reorder?

any: a buffer holding a key, password or secret is cleared with a plain memset or loop just before it is freed or goes out of scope
a constant-time comparison or check relies on code the optimiser may short-circuit
a security check relies on undefined behaviour, such as testing for signed overflow or a pointer wrapping after it has occurred
c: memory ordering for a security flag shared between threads relies on plain variables without volatile, atomics or barriers
cpp: a secret in a std::string, std::vector or std::array is cleared with std::fill or memset just before it is destroyed

any: secrets are cleared with an API guaranteed not to be elided, such as explicit_bzero, memset_s, SecureZeroMemory or a zeroize crate
comparisons use a library constant-time function
the function has no security-relevant step that depends on code surviving optimisation
cpp: a flag shared between threads is a std::atomic, and secrets are wiped with a non-elidable call such as OPENSSL_cleanse on data()
python: ordinary Python code, where no ahead-of-time optimiser removes stores; clearing may still be ineffective for other reasons
javascript: ordinary JavaScript where no secret clearing or timing-safe logic is present
